summary: Gives recommendations to help implementers of IMAP4 clients and servers, since the protocol is rich and offers many choices and trade-offs. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: IMAP has lots of options, so this is a tips sheet from experts on avoiding common mistakes.

subtitle: Practical advice for IMAP4 client and server authors on the traps that break interoperability.

tldr.problem: IMAP4 is a rich protocol with many implementation choices, so clients and servers made independently often trip over each other.
tldr.mechanism: The memo walks through accessibility, scaling, avoiding invalid requests and a list of protocol pitfalls, giving must, should and may recommendations for each.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo, not a standard. It has been updated by RFC 7162, and its advice is aimed at making the end products as interoperable as possible.

today: RFC 2683 is an Informational memo, not a standard, and it is updated by RFC 7162. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Purpose and the Meaning of Must and Should
sections.content:
The IMAP4 specification (RFC 2060) describes a rich protocol for storing, retrieving and manipulating electronic mail. Because there are so many implementation choices, the memo outlines the trade-offs and makes recommendations so end products interoperate.

It uses lowercase must, should and may with its own meanings, not exactly those of RFC 2119. must is necessary for interoperability; should is strongly recommended and not to be ignored without careful consideration; may marks an acceptable choice. In the examples, C: is a line sent by the client and S: a line sent by the server.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a tips sheet for people writing mail programs. Its words like 'must' and 'should' tell you how important each tip is.

sections.title: Shared Mailboxes and Severed Connections
sections.content:
Unlike POP3, IMAP4 permits several simultaneous accesses to one mailbox, but no server is guaranteed to support it. A client must not assume it can open the same mailbox twice: it must handle a refused SELECT, handle being forced off if the server allows the second one, avoid making multiple connections to the same mailbox, and avoid STATUS on the mailbox it has selected.

A client that finishes should send LOGOUT, wait for the tagged response and close the socket. The memo admits there is disagreement about this, so servers must expect clients that just close the socket. Either way, the server should not implicitly expunge messages; that takes an explicit CLOSE or EXPUNGE.

A server closing a connection should first send an untagged BYE with a human-readable explanation. Inactivity timeouts are allowed but, as RFC 2060 specifies, must not happen before at least 30 minutes of inactivity. A client that knows this need not poll more often than, say, every 25 minutes.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not assume two people can open the same mailbox at once, and say goodbye properly when you leave. A server should wait a good long while before hanging up on someone who has gone quiet.

sections.title: Flood Control and Scaling
sections.content:
A client can ask for responses too large to handle. The memo's advice is to ask for less at a time. Do not use LIST "" *, since some servers expose circular hierarchies; list one level at a time with %. Servers that may export circular hierarchies should limit depth, and a suggested limit is 20 hierarchy levels. Fetch message lists in batches such as 1:50, then 51:100, or only from the first unseen message, and fetch large body parts in partial pieces.

Prefer selective fetches of body parts over fetching whole messages, and weigh the cost of FETCH BODYSTRUCTURE (needed for a paperclip icon) against its parsing time on large mailboxes.

For commands, a client should keep command lines to about 1000 octets (not counting literals) by using ranges like 1:286,288:10000; a naive enumeration of 10,000 messages gives a line of almost 49,000 octets. A server should accept at least 8000 octets and send BAD for commands that exceed its limit.

Clients should also offer subscribed-only views using LSUB. Flag searches such as UNSEEN should be fast because clients use them themselves, while user-initiated text searches can be slower, and servers should support CHARSET UTF-8 in searches.
sections.plainLanguage: Ask for a big pile of mail a little at a time, like taking a few books off the shelf instead of the whole library, so the other side does not get swamped.

sections.title: Using Capabilities and Obeying the Server
sections.content:
Clients should use CAPABILITY to learn which IMAP version and optional features a server supports, and should not probe by sending commands. They should not send IMAP4rev1 commands to a server that does not advertise IMAP4rev1.

When a server says what a mailbox allows, believe it. Do not SELECT a mailbox flagged \Noselect, do not CREATE a sub-mailbox in one flagged \Noinferiors, do not try to create a missing target mailbox after a failed COPY or APPEND unless the server returned [TRYCREATE], and do not expunge a mailbox opened with [READ-ONLY].

The final recommendation of the memo is: test against everything. Test a client against every server you can get an account on and a server against every client, including the reference implementations the memo names (the PINE client, the University of Washington server and the Cyrus server).
sections.plainLanguage: Read the sign on the door before you try the door. If the server says you cannot do something, do not try it anyway, and test your program with many different partners.

sections.title: Protocol Pitfalls
sections.content:
Section 3.4 collects the misunderstandings that have caused real interoperability problems.

  • Strict grammar: do not add blank space "for readability". The INTERNALDATE string is not an RFC 822 date string.
  • Special characters: double quote and backslash must be escaped in a quoted string or sent as a literal; CR and LF only in literals. Mailbox names use modified UTF-7. Clients must not restrict what a user types in a userid or password, since some servers use @ in user names.
  • UIDs and UIDVALIDITY: servers should keep UIDs permanently, and otherwise must change UIDVALIDITY whenever UIDs may have become invalid. Clients must then discard cached UIDs. UIDVALIDITY plus UID is not a unique message identifier across mailboxes, and making UIDs global limits their life unnecessarily.
  • FETCH responses: may come in any order, in pieces, or with unrequested data, so clients must be ready for any FETCH response at any time.
  • RFC822.SIZE: must be exact. Estimating it is a protocol violation.
  • Reference names in LIST work like a Unix cd. Clients should end the reference with the hierarchy delimiter, and servers must not insert a second delimiter.
  • Hierarchy delimiters: servers should use /, \ or .; other characters are strongly discouraged.
  • Other items: clients must present ALERT text clearly to the user, must not require special-use mailboxes such as Trash to be creatable, and should close a selected mailbox before deleting it. A server should permit deleting a non-empty mailbox.
sections.plainLanguage: This is the list of classic slip-ups: typing the wrong format, forgetting to escape special characters, trusting out-of-date ticket numbers, and guessing a size instead of counting it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The memo adds no security mechanism of its own. It describes the behaviour of clients and servers that use IMAP4, and so it has the same security considerations as RFC 2060.
sections.plainLanguage: This tips sheet adds no new safety rules. The safety rules are the ones already in the main IMAP rulebook.

viz.caption: BATCHED FETCH, ADAPTED FROM THE RFC'S EXAMPLE

data.title: Fetch a large mailbox in pieces
data.code:
C: 004 FETCH 1:50 ALL
S: * 1 FETCH ...etc...
S: 004 OK done
C: 005 FETCH 51:100 ALL
S: * 51 FETCH ...etc...
S: 005 OK done
C: 006 FETCH 101:150 ALL
...etc...
